title: Two Divisions, One Total
statement: For positive integers $n$ and $d$, there are unique integers $q \ge 0$ and $r$ with $n = dq + r$ and $0 \le r < d$; these are the quotient and remainder when $n$ is divided by $d$. Find the largest positive integer $n$ such that the sum of the quotient and remainder when $n$ is divided by $21$ equals the sum of the quotient and remainder when $n$ is divided by $29$.
hints: Call the two quotients $a$ and $c$. The remainder on division by $21$ is $n - 21a$, so try writing each sum of quotient and remainder using only $n$ and the quotient.

The two sums are $n - 20a$ and $n - 28c$, so $n$ cancels from the condition. This leaves a linear Diophantine equation in the quotients $a$ and $c$. Solve it using the coprimality of the coefficients once they are reduced.

The equation $5a = 7c$ forces $a = 7k$ and $c = 5k$ for an integer $k \ge 0$. The remainders are then $n - 147k$ and $n - 145k$, and these must satisfy $n - 147k \ge 0$ and $n - 145k \le 28$. Combine these two inequalities to bound $k$, then use the bound to find the largest possible $n$.
solution: Let $a$ and $r$ be the quotient and remainder when $n$ is divided by $21$, and let $c$ and $s$ be the quotient and remainder when $n$ is divided by $29$. Since $r = n - 21a$ and $s = n - 29c$, we have $a + r = n - 20a$ and $c + s = n - 28c$. The condition $a + r = c + s$ is therefore equivalent to $20a = 28c$, that is, $5a = 7c$. Thus $7$ divides $5a$. Since $7$ and $5$ are coprime, $7$ divides $a$, so $a = 7k$ for some integer $k \ge 0$. Substituting into $5a = 7c$ gives $c = 5k$. Hence $r = n - 147k$ and $s = n - 145k$. The bounds $r \ge 0$ and $s \le 28$ give $147k \le n \le 145k + 28$. Therefore $147k \le 145k + 28$, so $k \le 14$. It follows that every solution satisfies $n \le 145k + 28 \le 145 \cdot 14 + 28 = 2058$. This bound is attained. We have $2058 = 21 \cdot 98 + 0$, with quotient and remainder summing to $98$, and $2058 = 29 \cdot 70 + 28$, with quotient and remainder also summing to $98$. The answer is $2058$. Why this works. linear-diophantine-solving, coprime-divisibility, bounding: cancelling $n$ leaves a linear equation whose coprime coefficients parametrise both quotients by $k$, and the remainder ranges then bound $k$ and hence $n$.
